item.title: [Guardian China] Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’ in speech
item.description:
Thanks for tuning into our live blog of the Apec summit currently under way in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
There is plenty more to come, so don’t go away, but here is a quick summary of what we know so far.
Chinese president Xi Jinping opened the Apec CEO summit on Wednesday with a speech calling for freer trade and greater cooperation around AI. “We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development,” he said. “We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.”
Russian president Vladimir Putin also addressed the summit, speaking after Ukraine destroyed the vital Kerch road bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war. Putin followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as “former hegemons”. He said Europe was in a “humiliating decline” and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed ⁠after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired, instead making his country stronger.
Xi and Putin headed into a meeting after their opening addresses, according to Chinese and Russian state media.
Russia’s president Vladimir Putin and Chinese president Xi Jinping shake hands prior to a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China. Photograph: Sergei Bobylyov/AFP/Getty Images
The much-anticipated trilateral meeting between US president Donald Trump, Xi and Putin will take place on Thursday. The three men are due to meet on the sidelines and potentially discuss Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, ⁠AI and nuclear weapons.

People march in support of Salvadoran troops deployed in Haiti, in Port-au-Prince. [Clarens Siffroy/AFP]By AFPPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
Thousands of Haitians have taken to the streets of Port-au-Prince to show support for soldiers from El Salvador, deployed by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs that control large sections of the capital.
Protesters on Tuesday carried signs reading “Thank you, Bukele” and “Long live Bukele”.
Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from El Salvador went missing during an operation by the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The latest Salvadoran deployment, although separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought additional reinforcements to combat the gangs.
Bukele’s hardline crackdown on gangs in El Salvador has broad public support but has drawn accusations of human rights violations.
On November 10, he claimed to have destroyed the “headquarters” of one of Haiti’s main gangs, releasing video footage of a helicopter attack.
Since then, Salvadoran forces, backed by Haiti’s national police, have taken control of a football stadium in the capital.
On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged all security forces in Haiti to prioritise the protection of civilians and to use lethal force only as a measure of last resort.
In the first 10 months of this year, the UN recorded 4,595 killings and 2,050 injuries linked to armed violence in Haiti.

Donald Trump hosts China’s president, Xi Jinping, at the White House in September 2026. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe Rafael Behr
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours
In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power”.
Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.
In Donald Trump, Putin has a ready supplier of balm to soothe his injured vanity. The US president has a shallow, venal concept of power. He is impressed by gilded palaces and heavily armed thugs. He feels thwarted by American democracy and envies tyrants who operate without equivalent restraint. Since Trump measures greatness in a country by its leader’s contempt for smaller nations and appetite for self-enriching plunder, he willingly promotes Russia back to the top tier.
That is the significance to Putin of a three-way summit with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. It confers trappings of parity with the world’s two genuine superpowers. That is a win for Russia, regardless of whether anything of substance is agreed.

Here’s the latest.
President Trump met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines in Manila on Wednesday ahead of a flight to the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he was expected to cap his whirlwind visit to Asia by meeting the leaders of China and Russia.
Mr. Marcos gave Mr. Trump a red-carpet welcome at the Malacañang Palace, complete with a military guard and a gun salute ahead of a bilateral meeting and banquet lunch. The U.S. delegation included Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
In his remarks to Mr. Marcos, Mr. Trump described the U.S.-Philippine relationship as “one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific.”
Mr. Trump was expected to leave right after, having spent less than 24 hours in the Philippine capital. He briefly attended a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders and also met with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India on Tuesday.
In Shenzhen, the president is expected to attend the APEC economic summit, followed by a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. Mr. Trump’s unpredictable agenda could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.
The brief itinerary in Asia appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.
Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.
The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. Watch: Marco Rubio says recent tech outages are 'completely unrelated' to one anotherByOliver O'Connell and Jessica LambPublished18 November 2026, 02:15 GMTUpdated 4 hours ago
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.
Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.
In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple.
Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor.
Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.
Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.
He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people.

Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."
Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.
The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.

Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist from Bahrain who helped lead the island nation’s 2011 Arab Spring protests and spent years in prison for challenging its monarchy, died on Tuesday. He was 62.
His family found him unresponsive at their home in Turkey on Tuesday morning, friends and activists said. The Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which Rajab once led as president, confirmed his death in a post on X.
“We extend our sincere condolences and heartfelt sympathy to his esteemed family. We pray that God may encompass him with his vast mercy and reward him abundantly for his efforts and contributions,” the group wrote.
Ebrahim Sharif, an activist and close friend of the family, said Rajab's wife and daughter took him to a hospital in Istanbul, where he was pronounced dead. He said after speaking with Rajab's brother that the family believes Rajab likely died of a heart attack.
Rajab for decades was one of Bahrain's leading human rights activists. He frequently posted on social media about Bahrain's treatment of dissidents, and was an unusually visible figure in a country where voicing criticism can carry enormous risk.
In 2002, Rajab helped establish the Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which became a platform for him and his colleagues to call for democratic reforms in the island nation, where a Sunni monarchy rules over a predominantly Shiite Muslim population.
He rose to international prominence in 2011 as the Arab Spring uprisings swept the region and demonstrations erupted in Bahrain.

item.title: [BBC World] As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByLaura BickerChina correspondentPublished17 November 2026
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

item.title: [BBC China] How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in MayByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished17 November 2026
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
A blow to Asia's AI boom
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan said it protested to Moscow on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japan's airspace off the country's southwestern coast, the latest incident fueling escalating tensions between the neighbors.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters the suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes early Tuesday near Fukuoka, long enough for Japan to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
Japan's government lodged "an extremely stern protest" and “strongly” demanded preventive measures be taken, Koizumi said. He did not specify the types of aircraft involved.
“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said. “It is absolutely unacceptable.”
The Russian aircraft flew across the Tsushima Strait, then headed south and flew above the waters between Taiwan and Japan's westernmost island of Yonaguni, Koizumi said.
Taiwan's defense ministry said Tuesday it detected two Russian military planes entering the island's air defense identification zone from the northeast and that the planes flew through airspace east of the island before leaving the zone south of Taitung County in southeastern Taiwan.
The ministry said it “employed joint intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance measures to monitor the situation continuously and responded appropriately.”

Japan urges creation of an Asian energy framework to counter oil crises
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has proposed the creation of an Asian energy agency to help countries in the region cope with oil crises, such as the shocks from the Iran warByThe Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 4:45 AM
MANILA, Philippines -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi proposed Tuesday the creation of an Asian energy agency to help countries in the region cope with oil crises, such as the shocks from the Iran war.
Takaichi called for setting up an oil security task force and a Japan-based version of the International Energy Agency for the region. She put forward the plan at a meeting on the sidelines of the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in the Philippine capital, Manila.
“We would like to position this as an Asian version of the IEA,” Takaichi said.
The IEA is a multigovernmental but independent agency set up in 1974 in response to a severe oil crisis in the early 1970s. It provides policy recommendations and helps to coordinate oil reserves of its members. The Iran war that began in late February has raised the sense of urgency over energy security, especially in Asia.
Japan would help lead an Asian oil security task force, along with the Indonesia-based Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, or ERIA, an energy security research organization, to develop rules for emergency releases and sharing of oil from national stockpiles, Takaichi told a meeting of the Asia Zero Emissions Community.

The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters
Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director of Megaspeed near the end of 2023, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS but it said she was still "practically in control" of the company.
Alice Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.
